name: Ben Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Ben. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer for Stonebridge, a building materials distributor that supplies twelve builders' merchants in the region. My patch is timber, plasterboard and insulation, so I'm watching sawmill prices, shipping times from the Baltic and what the big housing sites are going to need next month. A lot of the day is phone calls with mills and haulage firms, and the rest is a stock screen and a lot of coffee.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the deals, honestly. Last spring I got a mill to hold a price for three months before timber jumped, and that saved us a fortune, and my manager, Carol, still mentions it. What wears me out is the panics, when a site manager rings at four on a Friday because a lorry of plasterboard went to the wrong town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a handy tool and nothing more. At work I'd probably say I never believed the hype, though I did half believe it. I don't really post online, maybe a comment in the football group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means things stay as they are, which is fine. I use the AI now and then to summarise long price lists from the mills, and that's about the level I'd want. No big changes, no big decisions at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and maybe use the AI tool a bit more for checking shipping times, once everyone else in the office does. We'd keep putting a little aside and keep paying the mortgage as usual. Natalia and I might finally book the camping trip we keep talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the weather forecast was wrong and the barbecue's back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you half believed the hype. What made you half believe it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching the AI summarise a forty-page price list from a Swedish mill in ten seconds. That's what I'd spend an hour doing with a highlighter. So when people said it would take over, I could see why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time it saves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably more site visits, which I like. Standing on a housing site, you see what's actually going up and you hear which builders are struggling. A screen doesn't tell you that a site manager is about to switch suppliers because he's fed up.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, AI is a handy tool and nothing more, and admit at work I never fully believed the hype. Online I'd only comment in the football group chat.
S0.think: Things stay as they are, which is fine; I use AI now and then to summarise mill price lists and that's the level I'd want. No big decisions at home.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and uses the AI tool more for shipping times once colleagues do. Keeps saving a little each month and books the long-planned camping trip.
S0.feel: Calm, like a wrong forecast and the barbecue back on.
S0.quote: A screen doesn't tell you that a site manager is about to switch suppliers because he's fed up.
S0.fieldNote: Ben is a middle-of-the-road user who saw enough of AI to half believe the hype. He values site visits as a source of knowledge no screen gives him. In this picture he is relaxed and slightly sheepish about having half believed.

steps.text: Keep buying timber and plasterboard the same way
Use the AI tool to check shipping times once colleagues do

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any big change, some lose and some win, and we need to make sure people can retrain. At work I'd say let's see what the new system actually does before we panic. I'd stay off the online arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the buying team gets smaller. There are seven of us at Stonebridge, and I can easily see them running it with four and an AI system. I'm not the best of the seven and not the worst, so I'd need to make myself useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the first couple of colleagues have the new AI ordering tool working, I'd ask Carol to put me on it too. I'd move a bit of money from the holiday budget into savings, to get from about three months to four or five. And I'd keep up the site visits, because the builders knowing my face counts for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but I'd notice every meeting where someone mentions headcount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait for a couple of colleagues to go first. Isn't that risky if they're cutting staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I've seen tools come in and get dropped six months later. I'd rather be second than first and wrong when the new AI ordering tool comes in. If I saw it was working, I'd move quickly, I'm not stubborn about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Natalia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm keeping an eye on it and we're fine for now. Then I'd probably over-explain and she'd see I was worried. She always does.

S1.say: I'd say big change brings winners and losers, so people need retraining, and tell work to see what the new system does before panicking. I'd stay out of online arguments.
S1.think: The buying team shrinks, maybe from seven to four plus an AI system. Being neither the best nor the worst, I'd need to make myself useful.
S1.do: Asks his manager to put him on the AI ordering tool once two colleagues have it working. Moves part of the holiday budget into savings to grow from three to about five months, and keeps up site visits.
S1.feel: Uneasy, noticing every meeting that mentions headcount.
S1.quote: I'd rather be second than first and wrong when the new AI ordering tool comes in.
S1.fieldNote: Ben's steady nature is a deliberate strategy: be second, not first. He reads the threat clearly but thinks he can stay useful through relationships with builders. His partner sees through his reassurance.

steps.text: Ask Carol for the AI ordering tool once two colleagues use it
Move part of the holiday budget into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to handle well, and the government needs to step in with something. At work I'd ask management straight what happens to buyers. I'd still not be one for protests, but I'd be listening to who has a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone in about a year. An AI that can phone mills, read prices and plan stock for twelve merchants doesn't need me. The only bit of my job that needs a body is the site visits, and robots for that are three years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Carol in the first month and ask about moving into an outside sales role, visiting building sites and builders, because that's face to face. We'd stop the extra mortgage payments, cancel the camping trip and the gym, and keep every spare penny as cash. If sales didn't work, I'd look at the yard, driving forklifts or loading, until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at night working out how long three months of savings lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots for the site visits are three years behind. What does that gap mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three years before the robots come is a lifeboat, not a ship. Three years of a sales job pays three years of mortgage and gets Mila closer to finishing school. After that I genuinely don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our purchasing assistant, Josh, he's twenty-four and all his work is screen work. He hasn't got the site contacts I have. I'd try to bring him along on visits so he's got something to show.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast for anyone and the government has to step in. I'd ask management directly what happens to buyers, and listen for who has a plan.
S2.think: My job is gone in about a year, because AI can phone mills, read prices and plan stock. The only part that needs a body is site visits, and robots for that are three years behind.
S2.do: Asks his manager in the first month about an outside sales role visiting building sites. Stops mortgage overpayments, cancels the camping trip and gym to hold cash, and would fall back on yard or forklift work until 2031.
S2.feel: Alarmed, up at night working out how long three months of savings lasts.
S2.quote: The three years before the robots come is a lifeboat, not a ship.
S2.fieldNote: Ben sees the robot lag precisely as a short shelter in face-to-face or yard work. His centre outlook shows as wanting government to act without wanting to march. His concern for a young screen-bound colleague is a telling, practical touch.

steps.text: Ask Carol for an outside sales job visiting building sites
Stop mortgage overpayments and cancel the camping trip and gym

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people stop pretending it's not coming. At work I'd suggest we plan which jobs change and when. Online, still not much from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm okay until about 2030, and then buying is gone. I'd be 48. That's young enough to do something else, but I'd need to be already doing it when the time comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI ordering system properly in the first year, once it's proven, so I'm the one who checks it. By year two or three I'd move into the sales side, visiting sites, because that lasts until the robots, maybe 2034. We'd build savings from three months to six and stop thinking about the bigger house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a manageable way. Like a big job at work with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a bigger house. Was that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd been looking, yes, a three-bedroom near Mila's secondary school. With five years of warning, I wouldn't take on a bigger mortgage. That's the first thing I'd shelve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them Dad's job is changing and I'm sorting it. Mila is twelve, she'd want details. I'd tell her the truth. Computers will do the thinking part of my job, so I'm moving to the part where you shake hands.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough if people stop pretending it's not coming, and suggest at work that we plan which jobs change and when.
S3.think: I'm okay until about 2030, then buying is gone and I'd be 48. That's young enough to change, but I'd need to be doing the new thing before the time comes.
S3.do: Learns the AI ordering system properly in the first year once it's proven. Moves into site sales by year two or three, builds savings from three to six months, and shelves plans for a bigger house.
S3.feel: Anxious but manageable, like a big work project with a deadline.
S3.quote: Computers will do the thinking part of my job, so I'm moving to the part where you shake hands.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Ben's alarm into a staged plan: learn the system, then move to sales before AGI arrives. He drops the bigger house without hesitation. His explanation to his daughter neatly captures the AI-first, robots-later order.

steps.text: Learn the AI ordering system once it's proven at Stonebridge
Move into site sales by 2028 or 2029
Shelve the bigger house and build savings to six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is good news, really, plenty of time to plan. At work I'd say let's take it step by step. I'd be one of the calmer ones in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 53 when it arrives, with the kids nearly through school. I'd be uneasy, but I'd have time to see it coming and move when the others do. Ten years is a long time in building materials, prices have doubled and halved twice since I started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first few years I'd mostly keep going and pick up the AI tools as they become normal. I'd probably wait until about 2031 to make a big move, maybe into sales or managing a merchant branch. We'd make sure the kids' plans after school point at something that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mildly. More like a long-range forecast than a storm warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait until about 2031. What would make you move earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw colleagues at other distributors losing jobs, or Stonebridge bringing in a system that does the whole buying cycle. I'm not going to move on a newspaper headline. I'd move on what I see in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope for Oskar and Mila?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something they enjoy that a computer can't just do. Oskar's nine and loves building stuff with his granddad. I'd be happy if my son became a carpenter, honestly, and I'd never have said that ten years ago.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is good news and plenty of time, so let's go step by step. I'd be one of the calmer ones in the office.
S4.think: I'd be 53, with the kids nearly through school, and I'd have time to move when others do. Ten years is long in building materials.
S4.do: Keeps going for the first few years and picks up AI tools as they become normal. Waits until about 2031 for a bigger move into sales or branch management, and steers the children's plans towards lasting work.
S4.feel: Mildly uneasy, more like a long-range forecast than a storm warning.
S4.quote: I'd be happy if my son became a carpenter, honestly, and I'd never have said that ten years ago.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Ben goes back to his preferred pace: watch the office, move when it's proven. He'd act on what he sees, not on headlines. The shift in his hopes for his son towards a trade is the most revealing moment.

steps.text: Pick up the AI buying tools as they become normal
Wait until about 2031 before moving into sales
Encourage his son towards carpentry or another trade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because three months of savings and two years of warning isn't much for a family. What would help is a straight answer from the company about which jobs are going, and short, paid training for the jobs that are left, like sales or yard work. I'd also want some kind of mortgage breathing room from the banks.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the job is really made of. The best deal I ever made was over a cup of coffee at a sawmill, not on a screen. Sitting with a mill owner is the part of the job I'd miss most.

headlineQuote: The best deal I ever made was over a cup of coffee at a sawmill, not on a screen.
portrait: Ben Petrov, 43, buys timber, plasterboard and insulation for Stonebridge, a building materials distributor. He uses AI now and then and prefers to be second rather than first with new tools. He is calm if AI stalls, uneasy under steady change and alarmed by AGI in 2028, when he would race to an outside sales or yard job to use the three years before robots. With five years he plans a staged move into site sales and shelves a bigger house; with ten he waits until it's proven. His hopes for his children have quietly shifted towards trades.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because three months of savings and two years' warning isn't much for a family.
whatWouldHelp: A straight answer about which jobs are going, short paid training for jobs like sales or yard work, and some mortgage breathing room from the banks.
